title: “I’m Already Stressing About Next Year. What Can I Do?”
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing as summer approaches and teachers begin anticipating the next school year, Stuart addresses anxiety about facing a room of unevenly prepared students. He argues that gaps in student preparation are a permanent, unremovable feature of the job -- not a new problem created by pandemic disruption -- because learning is a partnership, not a standardized upload, and no two students have ever arrived identically prepared. His reassurance is that the fundamentals of good teaching (high challenge paired with high support, credibility, understanding how students learn) have not changed even though the surrounding world has. He closes by naming the specific capacities -- clarity, satisficing, strong boundaries, and trust in unseen impact -- that will still matter most going into the next year, while acknowledging the work ahead will demand real effort.
points: Central reframe: gaps in student preparation are a permanent feature of teaching, not a pandemic-specific crisis -- 'no classroom has ever contained identically prepared students.'

Stuart's reassurance rests on continuity, not change: 'human beings are not different creatures than they were two autumns ago,' so the fundamentals of high-challenge/high-support teaching still apply.

He explicitly names four things that will matter most going into the coming year: clarity of purpose, satisficing (not perfectionism), firm boundaries, and trust that teaching works in ways teachers can't always see.
He frames the response to anxiety about the future not as denial of difficulty but as redirection toward what remains constant and controllable.
quotes: I'd like to speak a bit into any anxiety you might be feeling right now about your adequacy for meeting the challenges ahead.

Here's my point: gaps (differences in preparation) are part of the job. Always have been. It won't make any headlines, but here's my prediction: 21-22 will only be an exaggerated version of this familiar challenge.
Learning is not the same thing as uploading files into the cloud; it's a partnership. Create all the standards you want, but you'll never fully standardize it.

I mean, c'mon — the world may have changed, but human beings are not different creatures than they were two autumns ago. We're still all souls comprised of thoughts, emotions, beliefs, bodies, and relationships.
Though gaps exist, the fundamentals don't change. And it's those fundamentals — the arts and sciences of the head and the heart — that hold the keys to remedying gaps in preparation.
It won't be a lazy person's work, for sure. Never is. Pack your hard hat and your work boots because you and I will be called upon to master the fundamentals in ways we've not been before.
